subject: comparing models with binomial variables - AIC, or alternatives?

messages.author: 21500bbcaab21afc
messages.subject: comparing models with binomial variables - AIC, or alternatives?
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to run a SEM model that has a binomial endogenous variable, and want to compare whether a grouping factor increases the fit or not.

As far as I understand, these models (due to the DWLS estimator?) will not provide AIC scores, which I was planning to use to compare models.

I have recently read Shipley's 2013 paper, describing a method to acquire AIC scores via d-sep test.

My question: would you recommend any other way to compare models with binomial endogenous variable in lavaan?


This is how it looks:


SEM1="

speed ~ fat + muscle + wing_length

endurance ~ fat + muscle + wing_length

mating ~ speed + endurance +
              fat + muscle + wing_length
"


fit.pooled = sem(SEM1, df, ordered=c"mating")

fit.per_period = sem(SEM1, df ,group="period", ordered="mating") 


# mating: binary response (yes/no)
# period: categorical factor (period 1 to period 6)
# all other variables are normally distributed

Thank you in advance for any suggestions.

Best,

Ned

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: comparing models with binomial variables - AIC, or alternatives?
parts: I am trying to run a SEM model that has a binomial endogenous variable, and want to compare whether a grouping factor increases the fit or not.  As far as I understand, these models (due to the DWLS estimator?) will not provide AIC scores, which I was planning to use to compare models.

The inclusion/exclusion of a predictor means the models are nested, so you can use a chi-squared difference test.  But your problem is that you aren't fitting the 2 models to the "same data" (at least not in the sense required to compare fit measures).  Instead of fitting one-group and multigroup models, fit them both as multigroup models.  In the first, allow all parameters to be free across groups (they will be by default, as you currently specify it), and in the second (nested) model you can constrain all parameters to equivalence across groups.  Then you can compare the models using the anova() function.

Terry

Thank you Terry, that indeed makes a lot of sense. I assume the extra argument I will use here is group.equal = .

A final question: to make the correct comparison for my case (i.e. whether the grouping factor increases the fit of the model), should I constrain "loadings", "intercepts", "regression", or all? (although the model with the last option did not converge).

Best,

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: comparing models with binomial variables - AIC, or alternatives?
parts: A final question: to make the correct comparison for my case (i.e. whether the grouping factor increases the fit of the model), should I constrain "loadings", "intercepts", "regression", or all? (although the model with the last option did not converge).

An omnibus test of equality of covariance matrices across groups would require you to constrain all parameters.   To make sure it is working correctly, I suggest counting the number of parameters in your single-group model, and making sure that's how many more degrees of freedom the constrained 2-group model has than the unconstrained 2-group model. 

But you can also test group differences of specific parameters -- perhaps as a follow-up test to a significance chi-squared so you can see which parameters seem to differ and which constraints seem tenable.  FYI, you don't have any "loadings" in your model because there are only manifest variables.  I think you want to use group.equal = c("regressions","residuals","intercepts"), but that might not constrain the (co)variances of your exogenous variables (fat + muscle + wing_length), assuming you want fixed.x = FALSE.  But if you want to treat exogenous means/(co)variances as known instead of random, then that's not a problem.

Terry
